extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, postsecondary instructors, and researchers in undergraduate mathematics education
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation of online (WebAssign/MyMathLab) versus traditional paper-and-pencil homework and of a blended-learning (Memphis Mathematics Method) instructional model, using exam performance, item-level outcomes, course evaluations, retention, and demographic subgroup analyses. Focus is on measuring learning outcomes, student perceptions, and implementation features that may mediate effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning outcomes: exam scores and item-level final exam scores
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure of learning outcomes chosen for this study is the student exam scores as well as individual question scores on the final exam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both overall exam performance and the proportion of students 'passing' individual final-exam items are used as primary outcome measures. Analyses compare these measures across sections (online vs traditional) to assess whether homework format impacts measurable achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passing threshold definition
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of this study, a score of 70.0% or higher on an exam was considered a passing grade, while an exam score below 70.0% was classified as failing (though a course grade of 60.0% or higher ensured that the student passed the course).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The binary pass/fail classification using the 70% cutoff is used for proportion-based analyses (e.g., proportion passing each exam or item). The distinction between exam-pass (70%) and course-pass (60%) should be noted when interpreting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical comparison of proportions (z-procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferential z-procedures for comparing the proportion of students passing in the traditional section to the proportion of students passing in the online section were used to identify significant differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Z-tests comparing proportions are applied to overall exam pass rates and to individual-item pass rates; significance (p-values) drives claims of differences. Small sample sizes limit power to detect small-to-moderate effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework format as controlled experimental variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework format (online via WebAssign vs. paper/pencil traditional) is the manipulated independent variable; sections were created to be identical in every controllable way except the homework delivery system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control measures included: same amount of time to complete assignments, same course value for assignments, identical exam content and schedule, same meeting times. Implementation differences to note: online students had randomized problem values, three attempts per item; paper students had a single submission but could earn partial credit. These implementation details are part of the treatment definition and must be considered when attributing effects to 'online' vs 'traditional' format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomization/variation in online problems to reduce copying
rubrics_metrics.description: WebAssign randomizes certain values within most problems to reduce the chance that one student can simply copy another student’s answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomization is an integrity/validity feature of the online environment; when evaluating effects, consider whether randomized values change the nature of problems or collaboration dynamics compared to identical paper problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity structure / number of attempts
rubrics_metrics.description: Students in the online homework section were given three opportunities to correctly answer each homework question, while paper and pencil students were allowed to submit only one solution to each problem (but could earn partial credit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple attempts and immediate corrective feedback in online systems are considered mechanisms that may increase engagement and learning; differences in attempt structure should be treated as part of the intervention rather than incidental implementation detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading method and automation
rubrics_metrics.description: All assignments were graded (either by WebAssign or by a grader) and counted equally towards the course grade; online systems automate grading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated grading reduces instructor/TA grading time and is cited as an administrative benefit. Evaluations should weigh potential trade-offs: time savings vs. effects on pedagogy, feedback quality, and student perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format suitability for computationally intensive items
rubrics_metrics.description: Computationally ‘expensive’ test items (e.g., repeated matrix multiplication) may favor students used to doing lengthy paper calculations; the traditional section outperformed the online section on such an item (Final Exam Question 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes that the online section's practice (with limited paper computation and multiple-choice/limited-entry online formats) may not prepare students for long paper-based calculations. When evaluating homework systems, consider alignment between homework modalities and assessment task formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format suitability for conceptual/probabilistic items with immediate feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Items requiring understanding of conditional probabilities (e.g., Final Exam Question 12) showed statistically significant advantage for the online section; immediate feedback on similar homework items may have improved conceptual understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate feedback and multiple correction opportunities in online systems can highlight subtle conceptual distinctions (a priori vs a posteriori probabilities). Evaluators should consider which content types are likely to benefit from the feedback affordances of technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student perceptions and course/instructor evaluations (IDEA Long Form items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Student responses on course evaluation forms (IDEA Long Form) were used to assess perceptions; example IDEA Instructor items: 'Displayed a personal interest in students and their learning', 'Provided timely and frequent feedback on student work', etc.; Course items include 'Amount of work' and 'Difficulty of subject matter'; Overall items include 'Overall, I rate this teacher as excellent' and 'Overall, I rate this course as excellent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IDEA items provide a standardized measure of student perceptions; the study found no significant difference in instructor ratings but a significant difference in 'course as excellent' (traditional higher than online). Use of validated course evaluation instruments allows comparison across implementations but may be influenced by usability/frustration with technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disconnect between achievement and student satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite descriptive trends toward somewhat higher achievement in the online section, the online section was significantly less likely than the traditional section to rate the course as excellent (z = 2.30, p = .021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should account for the possibility that technology-improved outcomes may coexist with lower student satisfaction—potentially due to initial learning curves, usability issues, or perceived effort. Investigate causes of negative perceptions when interpreting efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample characteristics and balance checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers compared incoming math ability (Math ACT scores), gender ratios, and reported minor demographic differences between sections; Math ACT means were nearly identical, but gender composition differed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing differences to interventions, report baseline equivalence (test scores, demographics). Unbalanced covariates (e.g., gender ratios) should be controlled for or discussed as potential confounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical power and sample size caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to relatively small number of students in the initial study (n=29 and n=27), results are preliminary; small-to-moderate effects may require larger samples to detect reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret null or marginal results cautiously when sample sizes are small. Plan replication with larger samples to increase power and permit subgroup analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement as an intermediate mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Online homework systems that allow multiple opportunities and immediate feedback may promote greater levels of student engagement, which in turn may increase achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider measuring engagement explicitly (time-on-task, submissions, use of help features) as a mediator between homework format and learning outcomes. Engagement metrics help explain descriptive trends that don't meet significance thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome measures for blended instruction: success rates and retention
rubrics_metrics.description: In the MMM evaluation, success rates (pass rates) and student retention are primary outcome measures; data cover 11,970 enrollments across College Algebra, Foundations, and Elementary Calculus from fall 2007 to spring 2010.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale administrative data allow detection of program effects and subgroup impacts (e.g., by course or demographic group). Use both achievement and retention as complementary indicators of effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity impact: closing achievement gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: An explicit evaluation criterion is whether the Memphis Mathematics Method (MMM) can close the achievement gap between Black and White students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess differential treatment effects across demographic subgroups to evaluate equity claims. Report interaction effects and subgroup success/retention rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blended instructional model structure (MMM)
rubrics_metrics.description: The MMM substitutes traditional lecture-style instruction with a brief introduction followed by a laboratory session using MyMathLab: instructors begin each class with a 25-minute lecture followed by problem-solving; over a 15-week semester students log 30 hours of class time practicing problems on MyMathLab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When implementing or evaluating MMM-like models, document class time allocation (lecture vs lab), stated objectives, example-driven instruction, and total in-class practice hours. Fidelity to this structure is a key implementation metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with cognitive and instructional theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The MMM is designed to reflect theoretical orientations (cognitive flexibility, integrating abstract and concrete representations, embodied cognition, inquiry and knowledge building) and recommendations to blend student-centered and teacher-guided instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the intervention's activities and materials map to the stated cognitive principles (e.g., worked examples, multimodal presentations, just-in-time supports). Consider proportionality between discovery and guided instruction per Mayer and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: MyMathLab learning aids (five features)
rubrics_metrics.description: MyMathLab offers five student aid features identified as fostering increased learning: (1) step-by-step worked solution of a similar problem, (2) video example, (3) just-in-time (links to textbook), (4) view an example (worked examples), and (5) ask my instructor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each feature is linked to specific learning mechanisms: worked-example effect, multimedia learning, just-in-time support, guided problem walkthroughs, and conversational help analogous to intelligent tutoring. Evaluation should measure usage rates of each aid and their association with outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technology for course management and grading
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to instruction, instructors use the MyMathLab learning environment for course management and grading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing cost/benefit, include administrative efficiencies (grading, management) along with pedagogical effects. Track whether use for grading changes assignment design or feedback timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-paced and individualized instruction affordances
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer instruction may be as or more effective than traditional instruction due to the self-paced and individualized nature of the instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the technology provides meaningful individualization (adaptive feedback, pacing) and whether students take advantage of it. Consider measurement of mastery learning progress rather than only aggregate exam outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation fidelity: instructor materials and class activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors introduce basic concepts in a short lecture that contains objectives, illustrative examples, and problems for discussion; the laboratory session requires students to complete classroom-based assignments using MyMathLab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fidelity by checking lecture outlines/objectives, examples used, in-class assignments, and whether students actually complete the prescribed MyMathLab activities during class. Implementation variance can explain outcome differences across sections.
